Loaves
lōvz
n. pl. (shaped masses of baked bread — the units in which our Lord's two great feeding miracles are counted, and the thing the disciples kept failing to understand)
From Old English hlaf, bread — the same word behind lord (hlaford, loaf-ward) and lady (hlaefdige, loaf-kneader). The Greek is artos, a cake or loaf of bread, small and flat rather than the modern risen loaf.

Biblical Definition

Loaves is a counting word, and the Gospels count carefully. “We have here but five loaves, and two fishes” (Mat 14:17); John notes whose they were — “There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes: but what are they among so many?” (Joh 6:9). Barley was the poor man's grain, and the loaves were small flat cakes; five of them and a boy's two dried fish fed five thousand men beside women and children, with twelve baskets over. Afterwards there were four thousand fed from seven, with seven baskets over. The numbers matter because the Lord Jesus later made an examination of them: “When I brake the five loaves among five thousand, how many baskets full of fragments took ye up? They say unto him, Twelve” (Mar 8:19), and having drawn out both totals He asked, “How is it that ye do not understand?” The disciples were at that moment anxious about having forgotten to bring bread. The word appears again in the parable of the friend at midnight — “Friend, lend me three loaves” (Luk 11:5) — the picture of importunate prayer; and in the loaves of shewbread that David ate, and in the one loaf broken at the last supper of which Paul says, “we being many are one bread, and one body”.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines loaf as a mass of bread when baked, and notes that the word originally signified simply bread.

expand to see more

LOAF, n. plu. LOAVES. A mass of bread when baked; a mass or lump, as of sugar.

The word is the Saxon hlaf, bread; whence hlaford, a lord, that is, the giver of bread.

In Scripture the loaves were small and flat cakes, commonly of barley or of wheat.

Five barley loaves and two small fishes were multiplied to feed five thousand men.

The shewbread consisted of twelve cakes set in order upon the pure table before the Lord.

Key Scripture

Mat 14:17 — "And they say unto him, We have here but five loaves, and two fishes."

Joh 6:9 — "There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes: but what are they among so many?"

Mar 8:19 — "When I brake the five loaves among five thousand, how many baskets full of fragments took ye up? They say unto him, Twelve."

Luk 11:5 — "And he said unto them, Which of you shall have a friend, and shall go unto him at midnight, and say unto him, Friend, lend me three loaves;"

Modern Corruption

The feeding is explained away as a miracle of sharing — the crowd shamed into producing hidden lunches — which requires the evangelists to be mistaken about the one thing all four of them record.

expand to see more

The rationalising reading of the feeding of the five thousand has been in circulation since the early nineteenth century and is still preached: the boy's generosity moved the crowd to bring out food they had been hiding, and the real miracle was the sharing. It is worth naming what the reading costs. This is the only miracle recorded in all four Gospels; John says the men counted five thousand and that the fragments filled twelve baskets; Mark preserves the Lord's own later interrogation of the disciples about the arithmetic; and the crowd's reaction was to try to take Him by force and make Him a king, which no picnic produces. A God who creates from nothing can multiply bread, and the sharing reading is not a humbler interpretation but a denial of the text by a writer who has decided in advance what may happen.

The rebuke in Mar 8 is the pastoral point and it is uncomfortable. The disciples, having twice watched Him feed thousands from almost nothing, were in a boat worrying that they had only one loaf with them. He asked them the numbers and they answered correctly — twelve baskets, seven baskets — and He said, “How is it that ye do not understand?” They had the data and not the deduction. That is the characteristic unbelief of a Christian who has been long in the way: not the denial of past mercies but the failure to reason from them, so that every new want finds the soul as bare as if nothing had ever been given.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English hlaf, bread; Greek artos (G740), a loaf of bread; Hebrew lechem (H3899), bread, food; kikkar lechem, a round loaf.

expand to see more

Greek artos (G740) — a loaf, bread; the word of “give us this day our daily bread” and of “I am the bread of life”.

Hebrew lechem (H3899) — bread, food generally; the second half of the name Bethlehem, house of bread.

Hebrew lechem hap-panim — the shewbread, literally “bread of the face”, twelve cakes before the LORD (Lev 24:5-6).

Greek krithinos (G2916) — of barley; the poor man's grain, specified only by John (Joh 6:9).

Greek klasma (G2801) — a fragment, broken piece; the leftovers gathered so that nothing be lost (Joh 6:12).

Usage

"“We have here but five loaves, and two fishes” — an inventory offered as an excuse."

"“How many baskets full of fragments took ye up?” — an examination in remembering."

"“Friend, lend me three loaves” — importunity at midnight."
